clue.text: Admission in tarmac cesspool

indicators.note: In says the letters wanted are sitting inside the words that follow rather than standing beside them.

parts.note: the run starts two letters from the end of the first word and carries straight on over the space

explanation.surface: A confession turns up in a cesspool under the tarmac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admission' reads as owning up and means the way in. The space between the two words is the cover, because the eye stops at a gap and reads two words instead of one run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Admission → ACCESS: the right or the means of getting in, admission in the sense of being let through rather than confessing.

clue.text: Flower spreading anthers much? My!

indicators.note: A spreading plant sends its growth out in every direction, and letters told to spread do not stay in the row they were given.

parts.note: thirteen letters across three words, the question mark and the exclamation counting for nothing

explanation.surface: A flower throwing its anthers wide draws an admiring cry.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthers are the pollen-bearing tips of a flower's stamens, so the fodder is already botanical and reads as description rather than material. 'My!' is an exclamation in the sentence and two letters in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Flower → CHRYSANTHEMUM: a definition by example, the big autumn garden bloom being one flower among thousands.

clue.text: Fondness won't begin to show delight

indicators.note: What won't begin has no start to it, so the word in front gives up its first letter.

parts.note: a penchant for something is a fondness for it, and this is the word the deletion works on

explanation.surface: Someone's fondness stops short of showing any pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Won't begin' reads as a refusal in the sentence and is the instruction. Penchant came into English from French and keeps its French shape; strip the P and an ordinary English verb is left standing.
explanation.definitionFit: delight → ENCHANT: to enchant somebody is to delight them, the old magical sense worn down to plain charm.

clue.text: Partners and advocates lacking opening

indicators.note: To lack an opening is to have no way in at the front, so the word in front loses its first letter.

parts.note: to espouse a cause is to advocate it, and this is the verb the deletion strips

explanation.surface: Partners and campaigners who cannot find a way in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advocates' is a noun in the sentence — barristers and campaigners — and a verb in the wordplay, which is where the clue turns. The two words share a root: both go back to a Latin word for betrothal.
explanation.definitionFit: Partners → SPOUSES: a husband or a wife is a life partner, the sense of partner that means the person somebody is married to.

clue.text: Sob about letter, it will prey on one's mind

indicators.note: Letters sent about go round rather than straight on, so the three in front of the word come out in another order.

parts.note: three letters reset in a new order
ESS is the letter S written out as it is spoken

explanation.surface: Somebody weeps over a letter and then cannot get it out of their head.
explanation.walkthrough: Letters of the alphabet spelt as they are said — ess, aitch, em, wye — are standard crossword material, and that spelling is the only way 'letter' hands over three letters. 'About' does the shuffling rather than pointing round anything.
explanation.definitionFit: prey on one's mind → OBSESS: what obsesses you is what you cannot stop thinking about, which is the nagging the definition describes.

clue.text: More promising when top's off tree

indicators.note: In a down entry the top is the first letter, and with the top off the word in front gives that letter up.

parts.note: a rosier outlook is a more promising one

explanation.surface: Prospects improve once the top comes off a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: Being a down entry is what makes 'top' the first letter rather than the last, and the surface hides that by talking about an actual tree. The answer is the willow whose long whippy shoots are cut for basket-making.
explanation.definitionFit: tree → OSIER: a willow grown for the pliable rods basketmakers weave with, so the definition names it by its kind.

clue.text: Establish a good start in the tennis match

definitions.note: The first half is a verb and the second a noun phrase, so the two cannot be swapped in one sentence; a tennis player who has taken the first set is described as being a set up.
definitions.meaning: to found a business or a committee and get it running

definitions.text: a good start in the tennis match
definitions.meaning: a player who has taken the first set stands one ahead, the best start a match offers

explanation.surface: Somebody is off to a good start in the tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are senses of the same two words, with the split falling after the first. The tennis half is spoken far more often than written, in scores given as one set ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: Establish → SET UP, the verb for founding something; a good start in the tennis match → SET UP, a player standing one set ahead.

clue.text: Disorderly empress, if idle, is always faithful in translation

indicators.note: A disorderly crowd is one with no order to it, and letters called disorderly are not left standing in the order they were given.

parts.note: thirteen letters spread across a comma, every one of them wanted

explanation.surface: An unruly empress is loyal enough whenever she has nothing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is the Latin motto of the United States Marines, and 'in translation' is the setter's warning that the definition is English while the answer is not. Thirteen letters of fodder for a thirteen-letter light is as tight as an anagram gets.
explanation.definitionFit: always faithful in translation → SEMPER FIDELIS: the Latin for ever loyal, with 'in translation' flagging that the answer is not in English.

clue.text: Brother has awful colic — from vegetable

indicators.note: Something awful is in a bad state, and letters in a bad state no longer stand in the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: bro is the everyday short form of brother
five letters put into another order

explanation.surface: A brother has a bad bout of stomach cramp after eating a vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: Colic is the gripping stomach pain babies get, so 'awful colic' reads as sympathy and is really the instruction. The dash does the work of a colon, turning the sentence's cause into the clue's definition.
explanation.definitionFit: vegetable → BROCCOLI: a definition by example, the green-headed brassica being one vegetable among many.

clue.text: Boring chopped meat

indicators.note: Meat that has been chopped comes out in pieces with no order to them, so the letters do not keep their line either.

parts.note: four letters, exactly the number wanted, taken as printed

explanation.surface: A dull plateful of mince.
explanation.walkthrough: Three words, and the middle one is the instruction: 'chopped' sits between an adjective and a noun as though it were describing the meat. The adjective wanted is the one used of a joke with no bite.
explanation.definitionFit: Boring → TAME: a tame joke or a tame ending is one with no bite to it, which is boring in the everyday sense.

clue.text: Thailand almost bordering on a continent

indicators.note: Almost a word is not quite all of it, so the last letter is left off.
To border on a thing is to lie right up against it, and in an across entry the piece bordering on the A is written after it.

parts.note: the article is a letter of the answer here, not joinery
Thailand was Siam until 1939, and the old name comes up one letter short

explanation.surface: Thailand all but touching a continent.
explanation.walkthrough: Siam is a crossword staple, so a modern country can ask for a name dropped in 1939. The small 'a' is material rather than an article — leave it out and the count comes up short.
explanation.definitionFit: continent → ASIA: a definition by example, naming the largest of the continents rather than the class itself.

clue.text: Had a fight and was thrown out

definitions.meaning: a scrap is a fight in British use, and to scrap is to brawl
said of a plan dropped or a ship sold off for its metal

explanation.surface: Somebody had a punch-up and was shown the door.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are past tenses of the same verb, and the joke is that the joined sentence tells a story. The fighting sense is the informal British one — a scrap in the playground, not a leftover fragment.
explanation.definitionFit: Had a fight → SCRAPPED, British informal for brawled; was thrown out → SCRAPPED, as a plan or a ship is discarded.

clue.text: Joins together furniture around end of June

indicators.note: What goes around a thing is written outside it, so the word in front opens up to take the letter in.

parts.note: units are the fitted cupboards and worktops sold as kitchen furniture, and this word opens after its fourth letter

indicators.note: The end of a word is its last letter, and that letter is all the clue wants of it.

parts.note: the last letter of JunE

explanation.surface: Somebody puts the furniture together at the end of June.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Furniture' wants chairs and tables, and the word wanted is the kitchen trade's own. The month is in the clue for its final letter alone, which is the commonest single-letter trick in the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Joins together → UNITES: to unite two things is to join them into one, the plain transitive verb.

clue.text: Unique person on holiday?

parts.note: one stands in for a person in formal English — one does one's best
a worker away on holiday is off

explanation.surface: Someone out of the ordinary is away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work: the second half paints somebody absent rather than defining anything. 'One' for a person is the formal pronoun, the one of one does one's best.
explanation.definitionFit: Unique → ONE-OFF: made or happening a single time only, which is what having no second example amounts to.

clue.text: Work problem for one rejecting motion

parts.note: op is short for opus, a composer's work
a poser is a problem that leaves you stumped

explanation.surface: A problem at work for somebody who refuses to budge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Motion' is the trap: it reads as movement and means the proposal put to a debate or a meeting. Op is the composer's opus, printed before the number on a score.
explanation.definitionFit: one rejecting motion → OPPOSER: at a debate or a meeting the motion is the proposal put, and whoever speaks against it is its opposer.

clue.text: Teams essential to chapel evensong

indicators.note: What is essential to a thing lies inside it, so the letters wanted sit unbroken in the words that follow.

parts.note: the run starts near the end of the first word and carries on over the space

explanation.surface: The sides a chapel's evening service cannot do without.
explanation.walkthrough: Evensong is the Church of England's evening service, and the two words sit together only to bury the letters across the gap between them. The space is the cover: the eye stops at it and reads two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Teams → ELEVENS: football and cricket sides field eleven players, so British usage calls the sides themselves elevens, as in a school's first eleven.

clue.text: Two cuts of meat wanted, quickly!

parts.note: a chop is a cut of meat, the rib or loin piece off a lamb or a pig
the count is two, so that same cut is written out a second time

explanation.surface: Two chops ordered, and wanted in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chop' is a cut of meat and also a pidgin word for quick, taken into English from the China trade, and the clue uses both senses at once. The exclamation mark supplies the impatience the definition needs.
explanation.definitionFit: quickly → CHOP-CHOP: the barked order meaning look sharp, carried into English from Cantonese pidgin and still used to hurry somebody along.

clue.text: Danger of going back into Somali Republic

indicators.note: To go back is to return the way you came, so the run of letters is read from its far end towards its start.
Into says the letters wanted are sitting inside the words that follow rather than beside them.

parts.note: an unbroken run straddles the space in somaLI REPublic and is read backwards

explanation.surface: The risk that comes with returning to Somalia.
explanation.walkthrough: Somali Republic is the country's formal name, which is why the two words sit together at all; they are a hiding place with a turn in it. Runs that read backwards are the hardest to spot, because the eye scans left to right.
explanation.definitionFit: Danger → PERIL: a plain synonym and the graver word of the two — at your peril, in peril of your life.

clue.text: Relentlessly pursue dog

definitions.meaning: to chase somebody without let-up, as the press does a public figure
the hunting dog of a pack, kept for following a scent

explanation.surface: Somebody is told to chase a dog without let-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog' is itself a verb for exactly this kind of following, so three words read as one instruction when they are two definitions; the split falls before the last word. The noun sense wanted is the pack animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Relentlessly pursue → HOUND as a verb, to chase somebody without let-up; dog → HOUND as a noun, the hunting dog of a pack.

clue.text: Send round objects

indicators.note: Something sent round comes back to the same place from the other side, so the word's front letter travels to the back.

parts.note: SEND with its opening letter taken off the front
that opening letter, now brought round to the back

explanation.surface: Somebody is to send some objects round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' reads as part of 'send round', the office phrase for circulating something, and is the instruction instead. 'Objects' looks like a verb and is a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: objects → ENDS: an object is an aim or a purpose, and ends in that sense are what a means serves — the end justifies the means.

clue.text: Record company's right for Middle Eastern potentate

parts.note: EMI is the British record company that owned Abbey Road studios, the label the Beatles recorded for
r = right, the short form used in directions and stage instructions

explanation.surface: A record label's entitlement passes to a Gulf ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters reach for those three letters whenever a clue says record company, so the phrase is worth owning outright. The apostrophe-s is possessive in the sentence and pure joinery in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Middle Eastern potentate → EMIR: the Arabic title for a prince or commander, borne by the rulers of Qatar and Kuwait.

clue.text: One Parisian fitting in poor taste

parts.note: un is French for one, so a Parisian's one runs to two letters
seemly behaviour is what is fitting for the occasion

explanation.surface: A Parisian is being fitted for something tasteless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One Parisian' is the standard way of asking for a French word rather than an English one — the nationality names the language. 'Fitting' is an adjective here, not the tailoring the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: in poor taste → UNSEEMLY: what is unseemly offends against decency or propriety, which is the judgement 'in poor taste' passes.

clue.text: Woman next to food shop turned and grinned

indicators.note: Something turned is set the other way round, so the letters built up in front of the word are read from the back.

parts.note: the deli is the shop for cold meats, olives and cheese
Ms is the title for a woman without saying whether she is married

explanation.surface: A woman standing by the deli turned round and grinned.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces go together in the order the sentence gives them and are then read backwards, which is why the woman's title ends up at the front. 'Turned' is at home in the picture — she turns and grins — and is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: grinned → SMILED: a plain past-tense synonym, though a grin is the broader version of the same expression.

clue.text: To oppose some chores is terrible

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it taken as it stands, so the letters wanted run unbroken through the words that follow.

parts.note: the run begins inside the first word and carries on over two spaces

explanation.surface: A complaint that some of the housework is dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: The hiding place spans three words, which makes the run harder to see than the usual single word break. 'Is terrible' is a judgement in the sentence and nothing but letters in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To oppose → RESIST: to resist something is to set yourself against it and push back, which is opposing it actively.
